paper_title: MUON-RT Reusing the Teacher's Trajectory for Momentum-Free Muon for LLM Self-Distillation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Self-distillation methods for large language models with an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher already retain a history of student updates. Muon nevertheless stores a separate momentum buffer, increasing persistent training memory. We propose Muon with Reused Teacher (Muon-RT), which reuses the teacher-student displacement to eliminate momentum buffers for hidden weight matrices. We show that this displacement encodes an exponentially weighted history of applied updates and smooths temporally uncorrelated noise under a local model. Muon-RT removes its radial component, normalizes it spectrally, and mixes it with the current gradient after Newton-Schulz (NS) orthogonalization. Under explicit regularity and alignment assumptions, we establish linear contraction of an expected objective-gap bound toward a residual error level. With Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Muon-RT improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.6 points with 42% less persistent memory, and over momentum Muon by 5.4 points with 27% less persistent memory. With Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) on Olmo-3-7B-Instruct, it improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.0 points.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Self-distillation (Shenfeld et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026) provides an effective approach to adapting large language models (LLMs) by using privileged information to elicit supervision from the models existing capabilities. The student learns from its own generated responses by matching teachers predictions conditioned on additional context. This formulation supports skill acquisition and policy improvement while helping preserve previously learned capabilities. Such retention is an advantage over conventional finetuning, which can cause forgetting (Biderman et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025a), recognized challenge when updating LLMs (Shi et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025b). Within this family, SelfDistillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) uses demonstrations to guide the acquisition of new skills (Shenfeld et al., 2026), while Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) extends the approach to on-policy post-training using feedback from successful attempts (Hübotter et al., 2026). In this settings, the teacher is maintained as an exponential moving average (EMA) of student weights, following approaches developed in semi-supervised and self-supervised learning (Tarvainen & Valpola, 2017; Grill et al., 2020; Caron et al., 2021). The teacher therefore evolves alongside the student, providing an averaged model whose predictions guide subsequent learning. Figure 1: Muon-RT with SDFT on Qwen2.5-7BInstruct. (a) Average accuracy over 2 datasets against memory per GPU. (b) Gain over AdamW in points. Optimizing EMA-based self-distillation incurs substantial memory costs because training must retain student and teacher parameters alongside optimizer state. Adam Kingma & Ba (2014) and AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) store two running moment estimates per parameter. Muon (Jordan et al., 2024) reduces this overhead by maintaining one momentum buffer per hidden weight 1 matrix and approximately orthogonalizing update directions using NewtonSchulz iterations. Muon and its variants have been used to train Kimi K2 (Bai et al., 2025) and GLM-4.5 (Team et al., 2025). Nevertheless, optimizing self-distillation with Muon still requires three persistent states for each hidden matrix: student weights, teacher weights, and momentum. AdamW requires four, including its two moment buffers. For example Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, momentum Muon and AdamW require 103.2 GB and 129.0 GB of GPU memory for persistent states, respectively, compared with 75.4 GB for Muon-RT (Figure 1). Existing memory-efficient optimizers address state storage through low-rank projection, quantization, or shared statistics (Zhao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025). The teacher offers another opportunity: reusing history already maintained by self-distillation to remove separate optimizer buffer. We therefore ask: Can the teachers existing parameter trajectory replace Muons momentum buffer reducing persistent memory while improving task accuracy in self-distillation? Why could the teacher replace momentum? In SDFT and SDPO, the teacher is not fixed; its weights continuously follow the evolving student through an EMA. Unlike momentum, which averages gradients, the teacher averages weights. The momentum-like information therefore lies in the teacherstudent displacement, not the teacher itself. As the student progresses, this displacement records an exponentially weighted history of applied updates (Lemma 1), smoothing noisy steps while preserving persistent directions (Lemma 2). Under gradient descent, this history is proportional to gradient momentum; under Muon, it captures previously orthogonalized updates. As optimization settles, the displacement shrinks as the teacher catches up with the student. Although this cannot recover AdamWs second-moment statistics, however, it can replace Muons momentum buffer. Even though this approach appears simple, reusing the teacherstudent displacement in Muon is not straightforward. First, Muon orthogonalizes its updates, so the displacement averages past optimizer outputs rather than raw gradients. Using it directly as momentum would feed these outputs back into the optimizer. Second, mixing the displacement with gradients before NewtonSchulz leaves its influence uncontrolled, as NewtonSchulz can amplify weak singular directions. This distinction matters in self-distillation, where the teacher and learning targets continuously evolve with the student. While momentum averages gradients from outdated targets, the displacement captures the updates actually applied to the student, providing different source of historical guidance. We therefore propose Muon with Reused Teacher (Muon-RT), which replaces the dedicated momentum buffer with information from the existing EMA teacher. For each hidden weight matrix, Muon-RT orthogonalizes the current gradient without momentum and separately computes the teacherstudent displacement. It removes the component parallel to the student weights and scales the remainder by an estimate of its largest singular value. The two directions are then combined after orthogonalization using small fixed mixing coefficient. This preserves current gradient information while adding historical guidance without changing the training objective. Only one small vector per matrix is retained to warm-start power iteration across successive optimization steps. The method applies wherever parameter-aligned EMA teacher is already maintained, including the studied SDFT and SDPO settings and mean-teacher training (Tarvainen & Valpola, 2017). Independent teachers lacking this alignment fall outside its scope. Our contributions are: We establish that the teacherstudent displacement stores discounted history of applied updates, is proportional to gradient momentum under gradient descent, and reduces variance under local model with fixed direction and temporally uncorrelated noise. We introduce Muon-RT, eliminating hidden-matrix momentum buffers through normalized teacher student displacement added after orthogonalization. Under regularity, bounded objective drift, and alignment assumptions, we establish linear contraction of an expected objective-gap bound toward residual error level. With SDFT, Muon-RT improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.6 points with 42% less persistent memory, and over momentum Muon by 5.4 points with 27% less (Figure 1). With SDPO, it gains 2.0 points over AdamW. Muon-RT ranks first among Muon variants across both hosts six settings.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We evaluate Muon-RT as drop-in optimizer for two self-distillation hosts: fine-tuning with SDFT and on-policy post-training with SDPO. Our evaluation covers task accuracy, retention of prior capabilities, convergence speed and memory. Finally, ablations isolate each design choice, and we test the theory of Section 3.4 against empirical measurements. 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Tasks and data. For fine-tuning with self-distillation, we follow SDFT (Shenfeld et al., 2026) on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2024a) with its two tasks: tool use from ToolAlpaca (Tang et al., 2023) and science questions from SciKnowEval (Feng et al., 2024). For on-policy post-training, we follow SDPO (Hübotter et al., 2026) on Olmo-3-7B-Instruct (Ettinger et al., 2025) with the biology and materials subsets of SciKnowEval. In both settings, we use the default splits and metrics of the original papers. Baselines. For SDFT, we compare with SFT, SFT with re-invoked prior knowledge, DFT (Wu et al., 2025) and SDFT with AdamW, as reported by Shenfeld et al. (2026). We additionally run SDFT with Muon and with MuonClip, which adds the querykey logit clipping (QK-Clip) of Kimi K2 (Bai et al., 2025). Both Muon variant use µ=0, their stronger setting; momentum µ=0.95 is evaluated as an ablation  (Table 3)  . For SDPO, we compare with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO; Shao et al., 2024), on-policy GRPO and SDPO with AdamW, as reported by Hübotter et al. (2026), and run SDPO with Muon, MuonClip and Muon-RT. The training and evaluation details are provide in the Appendix A.9 and Appendix A.5 lists all hyperparameter settings. 6 Figure 3: Training dynamics with SDFT. sections.title: 4.4 MEMORY AND COMPUTE
sections.content: Figure 3(d) reports persistent memory per GPU, measured between steps when gradients are freed, with every optimizer using 32-bit EMAteacher. Because Muon-RT keeps no optimizer state for hidden matrices, it needs only 37.7 GB, 13.9 GB (27%) less than Muon with its standard momentum µ=0.95 and 26.8 GB (42%) less than AdamW. Momentum-free Muon and MuonClip need the same 37.7 GB but are 0.85.1 points less accurate  (Table 1)  : Muon-RT therefore obtains the benefit of momentum without storing momentum buffer. At 10T parameters, Muon-RT needs 121 TB, 25% less than Muon or MuonClip with momentum (160 TB) and 40% less than AdamW (200 TB; Figure 5, Appendix A.6). The additional cost is one power iteration and one extra gather per matrix. The optimizer step takes 2.3 s, about 2% of training step dominated by generation. Figure 5: Projected persistent memory of self-distillation versus model size, with all states in 32 bits and gradients included. 4.5 ABLATIONS AND ANALYSIS We ablate each component of Muon-RT with SDFT on both tasks  (Table 3)  : the optimizer state it replaces, the teacher weight α, the construction of the teacher branch, and its combination with logit clipping. All ablations follow the setting of Table 1, with α=0.1 unless varied, and every block includes the full method as reference. The Appendix A.11 provides the detailed discussion about the ablation provide in the Table 1. 4.6 EMPIRICAL CHECKS OF THE THEORY Figure 4 tests each theoretical statement with matching measurement. The details are discussed in the Appendix A.10 where we empirically justify each theoretical claims.

Training on the models own samples against teacher improves adaptation (Agarwal et al., 2024; Ko et al., 2024), with further advances in 8 self-distillation (Xu et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2023). Such approaches can reduce forgetting relative to SFT (Yang et al., 2024b; Shenfeld et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025), which often compromises prior capabilities (Biderman et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025a; Shi et al., 2025). In particular, SDFT (Shenfeld et al., 2026) and SDPO (Hübotter et al., 2026) use privileged context with an EMAteacher. These methods redesign the objective but retain standard optimizers, keeping 2 model-sized histories without exploiting their interaction. We preserve their objectives and modify only the optimizer, improving accuracy with both hosts. Muon (Jordan et al., 2024) brings orthogonalized updates to LLMs (Liu et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2025), supported by analyses of matrix updates (Amsel et al., 2025; Large et al., 2024) and of its convergence (Li & Hong, 2025; Shen et al., 2025). Other optimizers include SOAP (Vyas et al., 2024), Sophia (Liu et al., 2024) and Lion (Chen et al., 2023). Memory-efficient methods use low-rank projections (Zhao et al., 2024; Hao et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025), quantized or shared states (Li et al., 2023; Dettmers et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025), block updates (Luo et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2024), or fused updates (Lv et al., 2024; Malladi et al., 2023). Others introduce slow averages (Pagliardini et al., 2025) or examine optimizer tuning (Zhao et al., 2025). These approaches redesign the optimizers own state rather than reuse model copies already maintained during training. Muon-RT eliminates Muons momentum state, saving 27% of the measured memory at 7B and 25% of the projected memory at 10T while improving accuracy. EMA-teachers provide stable learning targets (Tarvainen & Valpola, 2017; Grill et al., 2020; Caron et al., 2021), extending to representation learning (Oquab et al., 2024) and EMA scaling (Busbridge et al., 2023; Morales-Brotons et al., 2024). Weight averaging also improves optimization and model selection (Polyak & Juditsky, 1992; Izmailov et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Jang et al., 2024; Ramé et al., 2024; Defazio et al., 2024), and momentum itself can be written as an average of iterates (Defazio, 2020) or mixed with the current gradient (Ma & Yarats, 2019). These approaches treat the average as model, target or dedicated buffer, without characterizing the information encoded by its displacement from current weights. We show that this gap stores applied updates, averages out noise, and provides reusable optimized direction.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We asked whether the EMA-teacher of self-distillation can replace Muons momentum buffer. We showed that the teacherstudent displacement is discounted sum of applied updates (Lemma 1) that averages out their noise (Lemma 2), while the orthogonalized gradient is already optimal for single step (Proposition 1); the teacher thus adds temporal information rather than better instantaneous direction. On this basis, Muon-RT drops the momentum buffer and adds the radial-free, spectrally normalized displacement after orthogonalization with bounded weight, with linear convergence under the PL condition. Empirically, it reached the highest accuracy among all optimizers with both SDFT and SDPO, converged faster with SDFT, retained prior capabilities well above SFT and reduced memory. The ablations show that gradient momentum hurts when the target moves, whereas the teachers history helps when it enters after orthogonalization and stays consistent with the student. Any method that keeps parameter-aligned EMA model can lend it to the optimizer.

sections.title: LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Our experiments cover 7B-parameter models from 2 families and 4 tasks; larger models and further domains are left for future work. The convergence analysis relies on smoothness, PL and alignment assumptions that are standard for non-convex optimization but whose constants are not estimated for LLMs. Muon-RT applies when parameter-aligned EMA-teacher already exists, as in SDFT and SDPO; for methods without one, teacher kept only to replace momentum would not save memory.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This work changes how model is optimized, not what it is trained on, and it uses public datasets (ToolAlpaca, SciKnowEval) under their released licenses and splits. Models trained on science questions may still produce wrong answers about chemical, biological or material properties and should not be used for laboratory or safety decisions without expert checks. Reducing optimizer 9 memory lowers the hardware needed for continual adaptation; we report our compute in Appendix A.5. AI assistants were used only for language and writing refinement; the authors checked all content and remain responsible for it.

Remark 3 (What the theorem does and does not establish). Corollary 1 supports two claims under explicit conditions: faster finite-time contraction and lower optimization-error bound. It does not claim that Muon-RT universally reaches better local minimum in an arbitrary non-convex neural-network landscape. Higher downstream accuracy can be consistent with the lower error bound and the temporal smoothing of the raw trajectory discussed above, but the mapping from optimization loss to task accuracy is dataand objective-dependent and is therefore verified empirically rather than assumed by the theorem. A.3 TEACHER PRECISION W(s) Muon-RT reads the teacherstudent displacement W(s) , so the teacher must actually follow the EMA of Eq. (3). With τ =0.99, each step moves the teacher by 1% of the displacement, and the displacement is only 0.10.3% of the weights (Appendix A.7). The per-step change is therefore about 105 of weights magnitude, while bfloat16 can only represent relative changes larger than about 4 103 (8 significand bits). In 16-bit storage most EMA steps round to zero. We measured this on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct key projection matrix with 250 momentum-free Muon steps (Figure 6(a); setup in Appendix A.7): the student moved by 2.15 in Frobenius norm, 32-bit teacher by 1.37, and bfloat16 teacher by only 0.66, with 79% of its entries never changing. 16-bit displacement would thus reflect rounding rather than the averaged trajectory that Lemmas 1 and 2 describe. For the same reason, optimizer states such as Muons momentum and AdamWs moments are usually kept in 32 bits (Liu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023); since the teacher takes over the role of optimizer state, we store it in 32 bits as well, and we do so for every optimizer we train in Tables 13, so that comparisons share the same teacher. The teachers forward pass still runs in bfloat16, so the self-distillation loss is computed as in SDFT. The 32-bit teacher adds 2 bytes per parameter (7.6 GB per GPU with 2 GPUs); the memory in Figure 3(d) includes this cost. Precision setting. Our precision differs from the original SDFT setting, which keeps the student and the teacher in bfloat16. To make sure that the gains of the Muon variants come neither from precision nor from run-to-run randomness, we train every optimizer in the same setting: bfloat16 mixed-precision student with 32-bit master weights and teacher stored in 32 bits, with forward passes in bfloat16. Lemma 1: the teacher stores applied updates. Eq. (7) predicts the size of W(s) from the learning rate and the size of the applied updates alone: it lies between the sum of their norms (fully aligned updates) and the root of the sum of their squares (uncorrelated updates). The measured displacement follows this range closely, with correlation 0.97 (Figure 4(a)). It peaks near step 107, after the learning rate peaks, exactly as an EMA of applied updates should. Without normalization, the measured size lies inside this range at every step after step 20, at 1.21.7 times the uncorrelated bound, so the applied updates share persistent component (Appendix A.7). W(s) Lemma 2: the teacher averages out noise. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct weight matrix trained with noisy gradients of known mean, the current orthogonalized gradient loses the mean direction as gradient noise grows (cosine 0.87 to 0.11), while the teacher branch keeps it (0.99 to 0.75; Figure 4(b)). Proposition 1: the gain is temporal. During training, the 2 branches are nearly orthogonal, with cos(O(s), P(s)) < 0.015 after the first steps (Appendix A.7). The teacher branch thus adds directions that the current gradient does not contain, as the proposition requires. Post-NewtonSchulz mixing bounds the teacher. Mixed before NewtonSchulz, even α=0.02 changes the update by more than its own norm, because NewtonSchulz lifts the teachers weak directions to unit singular value (Figure 4(c)). Mixed after NewtonSchulz, as in Muon-RT, the change grows linearly with α, as Eq. (11) guarantees. Theorem 1 and Corollary 1: faster convergence. Under the PL condition, smaller gradient norm means smaller optimality gap. At the same learning rate, Muon-RT has the lowest gradient norm from step 40 onward (Figure 4(d)) and the lowest self-distillation KL for most of training (Figure 3(c)), and it reaches its best accuracy earlier (Figure 3(a)). These observations are consistent with the corollary.
